item.title: Drupal Security Team Warns Second RCE Flaw Is Actively Exploited
item.description:
Drupal Security Team Warns Second RCE Flaw Is Actively Exploited

The Drupal security team announced that attackers are exploiting a second critical vulnerability that allows them to breach and hijack unpatched websites. This follows the recent patching of a remote code execution flaw known as CVE-2026-132165, or Fail2Install, which allowed anonymous users to take over vulnerable sites by abusing the Drupal installer. An update to the original security advisory warned that threat actors began exploiting the initial flaw one day after patches were released.

🧩 The New Vulnerability

The new security issue, tracked as CVE-2026-136716, was patched one week after the initial release. It addresses attack vectors that were left unpatched in the previous advisory and also enables attackers to hijack vulnerable Drupal sites. While most installations are covered by the patch, certain sites in unusual or incomplete install states remain vulnerable to site takeover, including production environments.

🔍 Detection Challenges

According to Drupal, it is not apparent in the user interface if a site is in the affected vulnerable state. Furthermore, sites that are already compromised may no longer be in the vulnerable state. The team emphasized that this issue is being exploited in the wild, and any site that left its installer remotely accessible following SA-CORE-2026-017 may still have been compromised.

⚙️ Recommended Actions

Drupal has warned users that any unsecured website may have been compromised and advised administrators to ensure the user 1 email address is one they control, considering a reset if necessary. Site logs should be checked for unauthorized access, with a focus on unexpected changes to or by the user 1 account.

For those who cannot immediately upgrade to Drupal 10.6.23, 11.3.23, or 11.4.14, the following mitigation is recommended:

  • Secure the installer on all new and existing sites by blocking access to /core/install.php in the web server configuration or the .htaccess file in the web root.
  • Follow the provided guide if evidence suggests the site may have been compromised.

💡 Broader Context

The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has flagged six Drupal security flaws as being abused in the wild since November 2021. Two of these flaws have also been exploited in ransomware attacks.

#Drupal #Security #CVE-2026-136716 #WebSecurity #VulnerabilityManagement

Source: Drupal warns of new site takeover flaw exploited in attacks

item.title: AWS Launches AWS-LC, a Standardized Cryptographic Library for PQC
item.description:
AWS Launches AWS-LC, a Standardized Cryptographic Library for PQC

AWS has released AWS‑LC, a unified cryptographic library that supports post‑quantum algorithms while maintaining compatibility, assurance, and performance.

🔍 Overview

  • AWS‑LC is a general‑purpose cryptographic library maintained by AWS.
  • Derived from BoringSSL, which originated from OpenSSL.
  • It provides hybrid post‑quantum key exchange via s2n‑tls for service endpoints.
  • It underlies aws‑lc‑rs (Rust), rustls, and the Amazon Corretto Crypto Provider (Java).
  • AWS‑LC keeps an OpenSSL‑compatible API so applications can replace algorithms without rewriting.
  • AWS uses it across its services; if you’ve called an AWS API, AWS‑LC was used on the server side.

🧩 How it Works

  • AWS‑LC uses formal verification to prove selected algorithm implementations correct.
  • It optimizes algorithm implementations to reduce latency and compute costs of new algorithms.
  • For TLS, AWS‑LC libssl keeps an OpenSSL‑compatible API; most applications that use OpenSSL for TLS build against it with small changes.
  • Applications that call libcrypto directly may need more work, as the API differs in places.
  • When new algorithms are added, s2n‑tls, s2n‑quic, aws‑lc‑rs, and the Amazon Corretto Crypto Provider adopt them automatically.
  • Hybrid ML‑KEM key exchange is enabled through existing TLS configuration APIs.
  • 1Password used AWS‑LC to move clients to hybrid post‑quantum key exchange with only a one‑line Cargo.toml change and no application code changes.

⚙️ Key Details

  • Three properties that reduce cost and friction of cryptographic updates:
    • Compatibility: update doesn’t require application changes.
    • Assurance: new code can be trusted when it ships.
    • Performance: new algorithm doesn’t add much computational overhead or latency.
  • AWS‑LC long‑term support (LTS) releases keep a stable application binary interface (ABI).
  • Applications link once, then take library updates without a rebuild.
  • One update reaches every application on the host when each process restarts.

🚀 Availability

  • AWS‑LC is available as an AWS‑LC library for C/C++.
  • The Rust bindings are available via aws‑lc‑rs.
  • Java integration is available via Amazon Corretto Crypto Provider.

💡 Why It Matters

  • Every cryptographic algorithm has an expiration date; traditional ones like MD5 and SHA‑1 have been retired.
  • Standards are revised and flaws found in implementations.
  • PQC is accelerating the pace of adding new algorithms and removing old ones to keep up with regulations and risk.
  • The move to PQC has government and regulator deadlines; PQC will progress in phases to enable hybrid and pure post‑quantum algorithms.
  • Each change reaches systems as a software library update; the practical question is how often you can roll out a new version and its cost.
  • By standardizing on a single library like AWS‑LC, organizations reduce ongoing responsibility and operational risk.

📊 Performance Impact

  • TLS1.3 setup time on Graviton4 is measured for different algorithms; the figure shows impact of new algorithms.

  • Client‑server architecture using hybrid ML‑KEM.

#Cryptography #PostQuantum #AWSLC #Security

Source: Make post-quantum cryptography updates routine with AWS-LC | Amazon Web Services

item.title: OpenNHP toolkit hides infrastructure using zero-trust cryptography
item.description:
OpenNHP toolkit hides infrastructure using zero-trust cryptography

OpenNHP is a lightweight, cryptography-powered, open-source toolkit implementing Zero Trust security for infrastructure, applications, and data. It serves as the reference implementation of the Cloud Security Alliance (CSA) Network-infrastructure Hiding Protocol (NHP) specification.

🔍 Overview

OpenNHP is designed to hide servers, ports, and domains from the public internet. In the AI era, visibility equates to vulnerability; OpenNHP inverts this model by remaining invisible until trusted. Consequently, scanners, bots, and AI-driven attackers find nothing to attack because nothing answers until a client proves its identity with a single encrypted packet.

🧩 How it works

The toolkit features two core protocols and a modular design inspired by the NIST Zero Trust Architecture:

  • Network-infrastructure Hiding Protocol (NHP): Conceals server ports, IP addresses, and domain names to protect applications and infrastructure from unauthorized access.
  • Data-content Hiding Protocol (DHP): Ensures data security and privacy via encryption and confidential computing, making data “usable but not visible.”

The architecture includes specific components that slot alongside existing IAM, DNS, FIDO, and Zero Trust policy engines:

Component Function
NHP-Agent Client that sends encrypted knock requests to gain access
NHP-Server Authenticates and authorizes requests; runs separately and is architecturally decoupled from the protected host
NHP-AC Access controller that manages firewall rules on the protected server
NHP-Relay HTTP-to-UDP bridge enabling browser-based agents to send NHP knocks via HTTPS
NHP-KGC Key Generation Center for Identity-Based Cryptography (IBC)

The workflow operates on a default-deny gate for every port, IP, and hostname:

  1. Registration (once per device): The agent generates its own key pair and enrolls the public key. The agent requests a one-time password (NHP_OTP), which the Server’s auth plugin delivers to the user (e.g., by email). The agent sends the OTP and its public key (NHP_REG), and the Server binds the key to the user and replies (NHP_RAK). The private key never leaves the device.
  2. Knock (every access): The agent sends an encrypted knock (NHP_KNK) to the Server. The Server validates the knock and sends an operation.

💡 Why it matters

Attackers can’t exploit what they can’t discover. NHP represents a next step in “hide the service first” designs, extending security stacks rather than forking them.

#OpenNHP #ZeroTrust #Cybersecurity #InfrastructureSecurity #OpenSource

Source: OpenNHP/opennhp

item.title: Microsoft Research unveils Magnetar: Faster, language‑agnostic zero‑knowledge proofs
item.description:
Microsoft Research unveils Magnetar: Faster, language‑agnostic zero‑knowledge proofs

Magnetar is the newest zero‑knowledge proof system from Microsoft Research. It can prove the correct execution of programs written in Rust, Go, or C, runs 10 to 39 times faster than earlier comparable systems, and its security relies only on standard hash functions.

🔍 Overview

  • Runs a workload and produces, together with the output, a short cryptographic proof that the program ran correctly.
  • The proof is small and can be checked in milliseconds by anyone, without rerunning the program, without trusting the prover, and without needing the input data.
  • Verification can be passed on to others who need the same assurance.

🧩 How it works

  • Zero‑knowledge proofs allow a prover to convince a verifier that a computation was performed correctly while revealing nothing about private inputs.
  • Magnetar’s processor description builds on the Phalanx idea of exploiting repetition in a processor’s instruction cycle to accelerate proof generation.
  • The system is instantiated with hash‑based cryptographic primitives, eliminating the need for a trusted setup and avoiding elliptic‑curve‑based constructions.

⚙️ Key details

  • Supported languages: Rust, Go, C.
  • Performance: 10 to 39 times faster on average than the prior fastest comparable systems.
  • Proof size and verification: Proofs are short; verification takes milliseconds.
  • Security basis: Relies only on standard hash functions, not on elliptic curves.
  • Zero‑knowledge property: The proof reveals no information about inputs that should stay private.

📚 Background

  • Zero‑knowledge proofs were invented in the 1980s; the concept of proving program execution has been around nearly as long.
  • Early practical approaches were limited to small programs and required either a layered sum‑check protocol or elliptic‑curve cryptography with a trusted setup.
  • In 2019, the Spartan system returned to the sum‑check approach, supporting general‑purpose programs without a trusted setup and allowing different cryptographic building blocks.
  • Phalanx (2021) demonstrated how to use repeated processor steps to achieve an order‑of‑magnitude speed improvement over Spartan.
  • Magnetar is the latest result of more than a decade of research at Microsoft Research on making zero‑knowledge proofs practical.

🔐 Security & Quantum Considerations

  • Many prior proof systems rest on elliptic curves, which can be broken by sufficiently powerful quantum computers.
  • Microsoft’s Quantum Safe Program aims to move products and services to post‑quantum cryptography by 2029.
  • Post‑quantum proof systems exist but often rely on newer cryptographic functions that have not undergone decades of scrutiny.
  • Magnetar’s reliance on standard hash functions avoids the unproven assumptions of newer primitives.

#ZeroKnowledge #Cryptography #MicrosoftResearch #VerifiableComputing

Source: Magnetar brings faster, simpler, quantum-ready zero-knowledge proofs

item.title: Concerns Raised Over AI Surprises and the Future of Public-Key Encryption
item.description:
Concerns Raised Over AI Surprises and the Future of Public-Key Encryption

A speaker has raised worst-case concerns regarding the future of public-key encryption in the face of rapid AI-driven surprises. The warnings highlight a massive gap between the speed of AI progress and the timeline required for humans to update security standards.

🔍 Overview

The core issue is a mismatch in operational speeds between technology and human standardization.

  • The speed of AI producing surprises and the speed of human beings replacing security standards are orders of magnitude different.
  • This discrepancy remains true even when humans utilize the very best AI assistance.
  • Recovering from a sudden cryptographic surprise is only possible if the preparation is done in advance.

⚙️ Key details

The speaker outlined specific probabilities regarding the breakdown of current cryptographic assumptions:

  • 1% chance we live in “Minicrypt”—a hypothetical world formulated by Russell Impagliazzo in which public-key encryption is impossible.
  • 15% chance we functionally lose confidence in our existing public-key encryption algorithms.

#AI #Cryptography #Minicrypt #Cybersecurity

Source: A quote from Matthew Green
